outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** After meeting a number of Black couples in crisis, Nisa Muhammad and Dr. Rozario Slack were inspired to create **Basic Training for Couples**.

Muhammad, founder of National Black Marriage Day and the Wedded Bliss Foundation, co-created the eight-week program, which educates dating, engaged, and married couples about the value of commitment, responsibility to the Black community, psychological differences between the sexes, sexual intimacy, and conflict resolution.

Slack developed the male-friendly portion of the program, while Muhammad created the female-friendly portion. Couples also learn about the history of African-American marriage, and many trace their own family trees for the first time to examine patterns of marriage and divorce.

The following is a rundown of the eight-week course:

### Class No. 1: Why Marriage?

This class explores the benefits of marriage for men, women, children, and the community. It also examines the history of marriage in the Black community, from slavery—when marriage was illegal—to current trends.

**Icebreaker:** A question-and-answer session about how the couples met.

**Homework:**
1. Choose songs that reflect the couple’s love for each other.
2. Create a marriage family tree.

### Class No. 2: From “I” to “We”—The Sweetness of Surrender

This class helps couples transition from “I thinking” to “we thinking.” It also helps them understand the importance of making their marriage a priority in their lives.

### Class No. 3: Communication—Getting Your Message Understood

This class encourages couples to take responsibility for their communication and teaches them skills to improve their communication techniques.

**Main lessons:**
- Respecting the differences between men and women.
- Learning to talk to each other rather than at each other.

**Format:** A teaching session with dialogue.

**Activity:** The talking stick. During a conversation, only the person holding the stick may speak.

### Class No. 4: Conflict Management

This class helps couples understand that conflict must be managed—or it will manage them. It normalizes some of the conflict couples experience while emphasizing that certain conflicts cannot be resolved and can only be managed.

**Lessons:**
- Addressing biases. When spouses have differing opinions, the stronger spouse generally wants his or her way.
- Learning how to bring closure to old issues rather than combining them with new issues or conflicts.
- Agreeing to disagree without degrading one’s spouse for holding a different opinion.

**Activity:** Participants separate into gender groups to discuss current conflicts. Each group works out ways to resolve the issue.

### Class No. 5: Let’s Make Love

When sex is good in a marriage, it accounts for only about 20 percent of what is happening in the relationship. When it is bad, however, it becomes a significant problem. This class helps couples address some of those problems.

The class approaches the subject from physiological and biological perspectives, focusing on differences between male and female bodies. The discussion also includes the chemical bonding effects experienced by women and men.

### Class No. 6: From Yours and Mine to Ours

Many couples in the Black community bring children from previous relationships into their marriages. This class helps them blend their families into one cohesive unit. It also discusses how to prevent in-laws from becoming outlaws.

### Class No. 7: Keeping the FIRE Burning

FIRE is an acronym for **Faithful, Intimacy, Responsibility, and Excitement**. This class helps couples maintain the FIRE in their relationships.

### Class No. 8: From This Day Forward

This class helps couples understand the value of commitment in marriage and encourages them never to make divorce an option. They create their own place for success.

**Review of all lessons:**
- Remembering that people gravitate toward applause.
- Finding ways to appreciate and affirm one’s spouse.
- Setting aside time for just the two of you.
- Learning to communicate so that your message is heard and understood.

### Bonus Class: Hot Monogamy

This class helps couples become comfortable discussing sex with their spouses.

### Graduation

The program concludes with a ceremony celebrating new beginnings. Couples testify about what the class has brought to their marriages during the eight-week period. The ceremony is a time of considerable emotion and bonding between husbands and wives.

Graduating couples are encouraged to bring a couple from their community or family who needs help.

(CNN) — Encounters with several Black couples whose relationships were in trouble motivated Nisa Muhammad and Dr. Rozario Slack to develop Basic Training for Couples. Muhammad, founder of National Black Marriage Day and the Wedded Bliss Foundation, co-created the initiative with Slack.

The eight-week course is designed for couples who are dating, engaged or married. It covers commitment, obligations to the Black community, psychological distinctions between men and women, sexual intimacy and methods for handling conflict. Slack developed the program’s male-oriented material, while Muhammad created the female-oriented content.

Participants also study the history of African-American marriage. Many create a family tree for the first time, tracing marriages and divorces across generations.

The course is organized as follows:

**Class 1: Why Get Married?**  
The opening session examines how marriage can benefit men, women, children and the wider community. It also reviews the history of marriage within the Black community, beginning with slavery—when enslaved Black people were legally prohibited from marrying—and continuing through current trends.

- **Icebreaker:** Couples answer questions about how they met.
- **Homework:**  
  1. Select songs that represent their love for one another.  
  2. Create a family tree focused on marriage.

**Class 2: Moving From “I” to “We”—The Sweetness of Surrender**  
This lesson guides couples away from an individual mindset and toward thinking as a team. It emphasizes the importance of making marriage a central priority.

**Class 3: Communication—Making Sure Your Message Is Understood**  
Couples are taught to accept responsibility for how they communicate and to use techniques that make their interactions more effective.

Key topics include:

- Honoring the differences between men and women.
- Speaking with one another rather than at one another.
- A teaching session followed by dialogue.
- **Activity:** Participants use a “talking stick,” meaning only the person holding it may speak during the conversation.

**Class 4: Managing Conflict**  
This session teaches that couples must manage conflict before conflict begins to control their relationship. It also reassures participants that some disagreement is normal. Certain conflicts may never be completely resolved and therefore must be managed instead.

Lessons include:

- Recognizing bias and the tendency of the more forceful spouse to insist on getting his or her way when opinions differ.
- Finding closure for old problems instead of carrying them into new disputes.
- Agreeing to disagree without belittling a spouse for holding another viewpoint.
- **Activity:** Participants divide into groups by gender and discuss current disagreements. Each group develops possible solutions.

**Class 5: Let’s Make Love**  
When a marriage has a satisfying sex life, sex accounts for only about 20 percent of the overall relationship. When the sexual relationship is poor, however, it can become a major concern. This class helps couples address such difficulties.

The material approaches male and female differences from biological and physiological viewpoints. Discussion also includes the chemical bonding effects experienced by both women and men.

**Class 6: Changing “Yours” and “Mine” Into “Ours”**  
Many Black couples enter marriage with children from earlier relationships. This class offers guidance on combining those family members into a unified household. It also discusses how to keep in-laws from turning into “outlaws.”

**Class 7: Keeping the FIRE Alive**  
“FIRE” stands for Faithful, Intimacy, Responsibility and Excitement. The lesson focuses on helping couples preserve these qualities in their relationships.

**Class 8: From This Day Forward**  
The final regular session reinforces the importance of marital commitment and teaches couples never to view divorce as an option. Participants establish their own foundation for success.

The course concludes by reviewing all major lessons, including:

- Remembering that people are drawn to applause.
- Finding ways to appreciate and affirm one’s spouse.
- Scheduling time exclusively for the couple.
- Communicating so that messages are both heard and understood.

**Bonus Class: Hot Monogamy**  
This additional lesson helps spouses become more comfortable talking with each other about sex.

**Graduation**  
The graduation ceremony represents a fresh start. Couples share how the eight-week program affected their marriages. The event is often highly emotional and creates greater closeness between husbands and wives.

Graduates are encouraged to bring another couple from their family or community who could benefit from assistance.

Basic Training for Couples, created by Nisa Muhammad and Dr. Rozario Slack, is an eight-week relationship education program designed specifically for Black dating, engaged, and married couples. The program recognizes that strong relationships require more than love or good intentions; they also depend on shared knowledge, practical skills, mutual accountability, and a clear understanding of commitment. Its gender-tailored approach allows participants to explore relationship concerns in ways that reflect the experiences, expectations, and challenges Black men and women may encounter.

Throughout the program, couples examine essential topics such as communication, intimacy, conflict resolution, and long-term commitment. Participants learn how to express their needs clearly, listen with empathy, handle disagreements constructively, and develop healthier ways of responding to stress. The curriculum also encourages couples to strengthen trust, deepen emotional and physical intimacy, and approach major decisions as a team.

A central goal of Basic Training for Couples is to help participants move from individual-focused thinking to a partnership-centered mindset. Rather than viewing the relationship primarily through the lens of personal wants, couples are encouraged to consider what will support the health and stability of their union. This shift promotes cooperation, shared responsibility, and a stronger sense of purpose within the relationship.

The program also invites participants to examine the marriage patterns they witnessed in their own families. By identifying both healthy examples and harmful cycles, couples can better understand how family history influences their expectations, habits, and reactions. They can then make intentional choices about which traditions to continue, which behaviors to change, and what kind of relationship they want to create together.

In addition, Basic Training for Couples places Black relationships within a broader historical and community context. Lessons on African-American marriage history help participants understand the social and cultural forces that have shaped Black family life. The program emphasizes that healthy marriages can benefit not only individual couples and their children, but also extended families, neighborhoods, institutions, and the wider Black community.

By combining historical awareness, personal reflection, and practical relationship education, Basic Training for Couples equips participants with tools they can use in everyday life. Its broader mission is to help Black couples build durable, loving, and responsible partnerships while contributing to stronger families and communities.

## Basic Training for Couples: Building Stronger Relationships, One Lesson at a Time

**Editor’s note:** Public descriptions of *Basic Training for Couples* do not consistently publish the program’s official class titles or a fixed agenda for the bonus session and graduation. The rundown below is a news-style overview of the curriculum’s reported core themes; details may vary by cohort and location.

For relationship educators **Nisa Muhammad** and **Dr. Rozario Slack**, marriage preparation is not simply about planning a wedding. It is about preparing couples for the decisions, pressures and responsibilities that follow.

Their **Basic Training for Couples** program uses the idea of military basic training as a metaphor: Couples develop practical skills, confront weaknesses and learn to operate as a team. The program is designed to move beyond inspiration and give participants tools for communication, conflict management, financial cooperation, intimacy, parenting and long-term commitment.

### Class 1: Defining the Mission

The opening class establishes why the couple is together and what each partner expects from the relationship.

Participants examine their definitions of love, commitment and marriage, while discussing the experiences that shaped those beliefs. Couples are encouraged to identify shared goals—as well as important differences—before those differences become sources of resentment.

The central message is that a successful marriage needs a clearly understood mission, not just strong feelings.

### Class 2: Knowing Yourself and Your Partner

The second class focuses on self-awareness.

Couples look at personality, family background, habits, emotional triggers and expectations brought into the relationship. The goal is to help partners recognize that disagreements are often influenced by experiences that predate the relationship.

Rather than treating every difference as a threat, participants learn to understand how two distinct people can build a shared life.

### Class 3: Communication Skills

This class turns to one of the program’s central concerns: how couples speak—and listen—to one another.

Participants practice expressing needs clearly, listening without immediately becoming defensive and checking whether they have correctly understood what their partner is saying. The session also addresses tone, body language and the damage caused by contempt, insults or emotional withdrawal.

The emphasis is not on avoiding difficult conversations, but on learning to have them without attacking the relationship itself.

### Class 4: Conflict Resolution

Conflict, the program teaches, is inevitable. Destructive conflict is not.

Couples explore common patterns such as escalation, blame, avoidance and keeping score. They are encouraged to separate the immediate problem from deeper issues involving trust, fear, power or unmet expectations.

The class introduces a more disciplined process: slow the argument down, define the problem, allow both partners to be heard and work toward a solution that protects the relationship rather than producing a winner and a loser.

### Class 5: Money and Household Management

Finances can expose differences in values, priorities and power. This class brings those issues into the open.

Couples discuss income, debt, spending, saving, budgeting and financial transparency. They also consider how household responsibilities will be divided and how major decisions will be made.

The larger lesson is that financial stability depends on teamwork and honesty. A budget, in this framework, is not merely a spreadsheet; it is a statement of the couple’s shared priorities.

### Class 6: Intimacy, Affection and Trust

The sixth class addresses emotional and physical intimacy.

Couples examine how affection, trust, friendship, sexuality and emotional safety interact. The conversation may also include expectations, boundaries, fidelity and the importance of discussing sensitive subjects respectfully rather than relying on assumptions.

The session presents intimacy as something couples intentionally maintain through attention, communication and mutual care—not something that automatically survives stress and routine.

### Class 7: Parenting, Family and Outside Pressures

Relationships do not exist in isolation. This class focuses on children, relatives and the wider family system.

Couples discuss parenting expectations, discipline, co-parenting and the challenges that can arise in blended families. They also examine boundaries involving relatives, friends, former partners and other outside influences.

The goal is to help the couple function as a unified team while continuing to treat children and extended family members with respect.

### Class 8: The Long-Term Marriage Plan

The final core class brings the earlier lessons together.

Couples review their communication habits, conflict plan, financial goals, family expectations and vision for the future. They identify areas requiring continued work and consider how they will respond when stress tests the skills they have learned.

The class emphasizes that completing the program is not the finish line. Couples leave with a framework for continuing the work after formal instruction ends.

### The Bonus Class

The bonus session serves as an extension of the main curriculum rather than a replacement for one of the eight classes. Depending on the cohort, it may be used for additional coaching, practical application, enrichment, relationship planning or discussion of issues raised during the regular sessions.

Its purpose is to give couples more time to apply the program’s principles and to connect classroom lessons with everyday relationship decisions. Because formats may differ, the specific bonus-class topic should be confirmed with the organizers of the individual program.

### Graduation: Celebrating Preparation, Not Perfection

The graduation ceremony recognizes couples who complete the course and honors the time and effort they invested.

Participants may receive certificates and share the occasion with instructors, family members, community partners and fellow couples. The ceremony also reinforces a central theme of the program: Graduation does not certify a perfect relationship. It marks the beginning of a more informed and intentional one.

For Muhammad and Slack, the broader mission is community-centered. Stronger couples can provide greater stability for children, families and neighborhoods. *Basic Training for Couples* therefore treats relationship education not simply as a private matter, but as an investment in long-term family well-being.

The program’s final takeaway is straightforward: Love may bring two people together, but lasting partnership also requires knowledge, discipline, honesty and practice.

# Basic Training for Couples: Preparing Relationships for the Work of Marriage

Nisa Muhammad and Dr. Rozario Slack created **Basic Training for Couples** to address a simple but often overlooked problem: people are expected to succeed in marriage even though many have never been taught how marriage works.

Muhammad, a marriage educator and founder of the Wedded Bliss Foundation, and Slack, a pastor, counselor, and family-life educator, saw couples entering committed relationships with love and good intentions but without practical preparation. Many lacked healthy models for communication, conflict resolution, financial cooperation, intimacy, and long-term commitment. Couples could receive extensive guidance before beginning a career, joining the military, or making a major purchase, yet receive little training before making one of life’s most consequential promises.

The program’s name reflects that insight. Like military basic training, the course is meant to build discipline, teamwork, endurance, and a shared sense of mission. It does not treat a wedding as the finish line or assume that affection alone will sustain a household. Instead, it helps couples examine what they believe, practice essential relationship skills, and create a plan for protecting their union.

The curriculum was also designed to make marriage education culturally relevant and accessible, particularly for African American couples and communities that historically have not been well served by mainstream family programs. Rather than describing couples only in terms of risk or dysfunction, Muhammad and Slack begin with their strengths: faith, resilience, family ties, community experience, and the desire to build a stable future.

Although particular workshops may adapt the exercises or combine topics, the course follows a week-by-week progression from understanding marriage to making a deliberate commitment to its future.

## Week One: “Why Marriage?”

The opening session asks couples to consider marriage before discussing wedding plans or relationship techniques. Why marry at all? What is marriage intended to provide to two individuals, their children, their extended families, and the larger community?

Participants explore their personal beliefs about marriage and the examples they observed while growing up. They also consider the difference between simply staying together and creating a purposeful marital partnership. The goal is not to pressure couples into marriage but to make sure that their decision is informed, freely chosen, and supported by a clear understanding of commitment.

## Week Two: Understanding Yourself

Before partners can function effectively as a team, they must understand what each person brings into the relationship. This week turns attention to family history, personality, values, habits, expectations, and emotional needs.

Couples identify lessons they absorbed—consciously or unconsciously—from parents, relatives, previous relationships, and their communities. The session helps participants recognize that many recurring disagreements are rooted not in bad intentions but in different experiences and assumptions.

## Week Three: Understanding Your Partner and Your Expectations

The next stage moves from self-awareness to mutual understanding. Couples discuss what they expect from a husband, a wife, or a committed partner, including assumptions about household responsibilities, affection, loyalty, work, faith, parenting, and decision-making.

Unspoken expectations can become invisible tests that a partner does not know he or she is taking. By bringing those expectations into the open, couples can decide which are realistic, which need to be revised, and which require negotiation.

## Week Four: Communication

This week focuses on the everyday practices that allow partners to feel heard and respected. Participants work on listening without immediately defending themselves, expressing needs clearly, asking questions, and paying attention to tone and body language.

The course emphasizes that communication is more than talking. It includes learning when to speak, when to pause, how to confirm what one has heard, and how to discuss sensitive matters without humiliating or dismissing a partner. Couples practice replacing accusation with language that invites understanding and problem-solving.

## Week Five: Managing Conflict

Conflict is presented as a normal part of intimate partnership, not automatic proof that a relationship has failed. The important question is how the couple handles it.

Participants learn to distinguish the issue being discussed from the deeper emotions surrounding it. They examine destructive patterns such as contempt, name-calling, withdrawal, threats, and keeping score. In their place, the program encourages self-control, fair rules for disagreement, repair attempts, forgiveness, and the ability to return to a difficult conversation after emotions have cooled.

The larger lesson is that partners should confront the problem without treating each other as the enemy.

## Week Six: Money and Shared Responsibility

Finances often reveal a couple’s deepest beliefs about trust, security, independence, power, and the future. This session invites honest discussion of income, debt, spending, saving, credit, financial obligations to relatives, and long-term goals.

Couples are encouraged to develop a workable budget and a transparent process for making financial decisions. The objective is not to impose one household model but to ensure that both partners understand the plan and accept responsibility for it. Financial unity, the program teaches, depends as much on honesty and cooperation as it does on income.

## Week Seven: Intimacy, Family, and the Life of the Household

As the course approaches its conclusion, couples consider the bonds that make marriage more than a practical arrangement. Discussion includes affection, sexual intimacy, friendship, trust, spiritual connection, and the need to continue nurturing the relationship after the wedding or after children arrive.

The session also addresses the wider family system: children, parenting, former partners, stepfamilies, in-laws, and community responsibilities. Couples learn that a strong marriage needs appropriate boundaries as well as supportive relationships. They are encouraged to protect time for one another while remaining responsible to the people who depend on them.

## Week Eight: “From This Day Forward”

The final week brings the lessons together in a forward-looking marriage plan. Couples review what they have discovered about their values, expectations, communication habits, conflict patterns, finances, and family goals.

“From This Day Forward” is not simply a ceremonial conclusion. It asks partners to translate insight into practice. They identify specific commitments, establish routines for checking in with one another, and consider where they will seek help if serious problems arise. The course ends by emphasizing that commitment is not only a feeling expressed once; it is a decision renewed through daily behavior.

## Training for a Shared Future

Basic Training for Couples rests on a hopeful but realistic view of marriage. Muhammad and Slack do not suggest that education can eliminate every disagreement or guarantee that every relationship will succeed. Their argument is that couples have a better chance when they understand the institution they are entering, know themselves and each other, and possess tools for handling the pressures that inevitably come.

The program therefore treats marriage preparation as both personal and communal work. Stronger couples can create safer homes, more stable environments for children, and healthier neighborhoods. By moving from **“Why Marriage?”** to **“From This Day Forward,”** Basic Training for Couples helps partners replace assumptions with conversation, good intentions with skills, and romantic hope with a practical plan for lasting commitment.

## Basic Training for Couples — Course Outline

*Basic Training for Couples* is a relationship-education program developed primarily for African-American couples. It combines practical relationship skills with historical and cultural discussion. The curriculum is generally organized around the following areas:

1. **African-American Marriage History**
   - Historical development of Black marriage and family life  
   - Effects of slavery, segregation, migration, economic pressures, and public policy  
   - Cultural strengths and traditions that have sustained African-American families  
   - Challenging negative stereotypes about Black relationships and marriage  

2. **Commitment**
   - Defining commitment and shared expectations  
   - Moving from an individual mindset to a partnership mindset  
   - Trust, fidelity, accountability, and long-term planning  
   - Identifying behaviors that strengthen or weaken commitment  

3. **Communication**
   - Recognizing different communication styles  
   - Active listening and speaking clearly without blame  
   - Expressing needs, feelings, and expectations  
   - Understanding verbal and nonverbal messages  
   - Creating emotionally safe conversations  

4. **Conflict Resolution**
   - Identifying recurring conflicts and their underlying causes  
   - Managing anger and emotional escalation  
   - Using negotiation, compromise, and collaborative problem-solving  
   - Forgiveness, repair, and rebuilding trust  
   - Establishing fair-conflict rules  

5. **Intimacy**
   - Developing emotional, spiritual, intellectual, and physical closeness  
   - Discussing affection, sexuality, and expectations  
   - Maintaining friendship and romance  
   - Addressing barriers to intimacy, including stress, resentment, and poor communication  

6. **Blended Families**
   - Adjusting to stepfamily roles and expectations  
   - Parenting and discipline across households  
   - Boundaries involving children, former partners, and extended family  
   - Loyalty conflicts and co-parenting challenges  
   - Building a unified family identity over time  

7. **Relationship Maintenance and Application**
   - Setting shared goals and creating a relationship plan  
   - Practicing the skills learned throughout the course  
   - Identifying support systems and community resources  
   - Developing strategies for maintaining a healthy, lasting marriage  

### The FIRE Framework

The course uses **FIRE** as a memorable framework for keeping a relationship strong. However, publicly available descriptions and different presentations of the program do not always give a consistent expansion of the acronym; versions commonly emphasize **friendship/faithfulness, intimacy, respect, and effective communication or excitement**. For the exact wording, the specific facilitator’s manual or edition should be consulted.

This is a reconstructed overview of the publicly described curriculum rather than a verbatim reproduction of the proprietary instructor materials.

counterfactuals.output:
## Building Black Love: Inside Nisa Muhammad and Dr. Rozario Slack’s Relationship-Education Program

For Nisa Muhammad and Dr. Rozario Slack, strengthening Black relationships requires more than celebrating successful couples. It means giving people practical tools before problems become crises.

Muhammad, founder of National Black Marriage Day, and Slack, a pastor, counselor and relationship educator, co-founded the Black Marriage and Relationship Education program to offer that preparation. Designed for dating, engaged and married adults, the program treats healthy partnership as a set of skills that can be taught, practiced and reinforced.

The course combines discussions of love and commitment with instruction on communication, conflict, finances, intimacy, parenting and long-term planning. It also places those subjects in the context of the social and economic pressures many Black couples face. Participants generally attend as couples, although individuals seeking to prepare for a future relationship can also benefit.

### The course, class by class

The titles and order can vary slightly by cohort, but the core program follows a progression from personal readiness to sustaining a marriage.

**Class 1: Personal readiness and relationship expectations**  
Participants begin with self-examination. The class asks what each person learned about love, marriage and gender roles while growing up—and which expectations may help or hurt a partnership.

**Class 2: Choosing a partner and defining commitment**  
The second session focuses on compatibility, shared values and the difference between attraction and long-term suitability. Participants consider whether they agree on marriage, faith, money, children and family responsibilities.

**Class 3: Understanding partners’ needs**  
This class examines the emotional and practical needs people bring into relationships. The goal is to replace assumptions with direct conversations about respect, affection, security, support and appreciation.

**Class 4: Communication and listening**  
Couples practice expressing concerns without attacking each other and listening without immediately becoming defensive. The session emphasizes tone, timing, body language and the importance of checking whether a message was understood.

**Class 5: Conflict, anger and forgiveness**  
Disagreement is treated as inevitable; destructive fighting is not. Participants learn to identify recurring patterns, pause arguments before they escalate, negotiate differences and distinguish forgiveness from ignoring harmful conduct.

**Class 6: Money, work and household responsibilities**  
The financial session addresses spending, saving, debt, credit, financial transparency and decision-making. It also pushes couples to discuss how paid work, housework and caregiving will be divided.

**Class 7: Sex, affection and intimacy**  
This class broadens intimacy beyond intercourse. Couples discuss desire, trust, affection, vulnerability, expectations and how stress, health, parenting and unresolved conflict can affect their sexual connection.

**Class 8: Parenting, family and outside relationships**  
Participants examine decisions about children, discipline, blended families and co-parenting. The class also considers boundaries with relatives, friends, former partners and others who may influence the relationship.

**Class 9: Protecting the partnership**  
The focus shifts to maintaining trust over time. Topics include fidelity, emotional affairs, secrecy, temptation and the daily habits that keep couples connected rather than simply reacting after a breach occurs.

**Class 10: Creating a shared vision**  
In the concluding core session, couples bring the lessons together in a relationship or family plan. They identify common goals, establish rituals for staying connected and decide how they will revisit difficult subjects after the course ends.

### The “Hot Monogamy” bonus session

The program’s bonus session, **“Hot Monogamy,”** is intended to challenge the idea that commitment inevitably leads to boredom. Rather than presenting fidelity merely as a prohibition, the class frames monogamy as something couples actively cultivate.

The session encourages partners to keep dating one another, communicate candidly about sexual and emotional needs, create time for romance and protect privacy around their intimate lives. It also addresses how resentment, exhaustion and routine can suppress desire—and why affection, playfulness and emotional safety matter to physical intimacy.

The tone is typically lighter and more celebratory than some of the core classes, but the message is serious: exclusivity alone does not produce closeness. Couples must continue to invest in curiosity, courtship and connection.

### Graduation: a beginning, not an endpoint

Graduation recognizes participants who complete the course and its exercises. Couples and individual students have an opportunity to reflect on what they learned, affirm their intentions and celebrate alongside classmates.

The ceremony also underscores the founders’ larger purpose. Muhammad’s National Black Marriage Day work has long sought to make stable Black marriages more visible, while Slack’s teaching emphasizes accountability and practical relationship skills. Graduation joins those two ideas: public celebration paired with private preparation.

Participants leave with more than a certificate. The aim is for them to carry forward a working plan for communication, money, intimacy, family life and conflict—and to understand that relationship education is preventive maintenance, not an admission of failure.

For Muhammad and Slack, that is the program’s central argument: strong love matters, but strong relationships also require education, practice and community support.
